before.label: Political history
before.description: Examines institutions, diplomacy and struggles over power through different methods. Namier reconstructs parliamentary connections; Benson studies voters; Tilly investigates collective claims; Hunt joins political symbols and social identities. Hill, Dorothy Thompson and Flexner examine radical and rights politics, while Guha and Cooper investigate insurgency and labor under colonial rule. These approaches overlap without replacing all earlier political history.

before.scope_note: Diplomatic, institutional, social, and cultural political histories persist and interact; the field did not disappear with the rise of social history. Distinguish institutional elites, electoral categories, popular organization and colonial subjects. Cultural political history can retain social and quantitative evidence; attention to popular action does not make all movements democratic. Regional examples are selective, not a globally complete political canon.

before.label: Biography / life writing
before.description: Uses individual and collective lives to ask historical questions about character, social relations, power and experience. Documentary reconstruction, psychoanalytic interpretation, contextual comparison and relational trajectories pose different problems. Authors, subjects, editors and collaborators shape the surviving account.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Ancient roots; Carlyle’s On Heroes (1841) is one nineteenth-century strand, not its sole foundation. Strachey (1918); Erikson (1958); Davis (1995).

representative_people.context: The opening Heroes lecture gives creative individuals and practical belief a large explanatory role. This is one nineteenth-century strand, not biography’s origin or all Carlyle’s historical writing.
representative_people.works: On Heroes (1841), Lecture I opening (5 May 1840)

representative_people.context: Selects compact portraits using French eloges models and existing biographies. Woolf later praises one royal biography while criticizing another; neither authorial impartiality nor a uniform critical verdict is assumed.
representative_people.works: Eminent Victorians (1918), preface; Queen Victoria and Elizabeth and Essex, evaluated by Woolf (1939)

representative_people.context: His 1970 retrospective connects his Luther interpretation with individual crisis and social transformation. The 1958 book has not been independently read; its original metadata remains separate.
representative_people.works: Young Man Luther (1958); “Autobiographic Notes on the Identity Crisis” (1970), especially p. 750

representative_people.context: Compares Glikl, Marie de l’Incarnation and Merian without making them one universal female trajectory. An explicitly imagined prologue tests her categories; stories, religious difference, colonial power and textual mediation shape interpretation.
representative_people.works: Women on the Margins (1995), prologue, selected Glikl opening, conclusion and acknowledgments

representative_people.context: Revises her assessment of Strafford in light of documents and scholarship; sympathy for subjects remains open to criticism.
representative_people.works: Strafford (1935); William the Silent (1944); Thomas Wentworth, First Earl of Strafford, 1593–1641: A Revaluation (1961)

representative_people.context: Collective lives form an argument against racist historical exclusion.
representative_people.works: The Black Man (1863)

representative_people.context: Uses a female sovereign to examine gender and power in a society restricting women’s political participation; a contemporary reviewer challenges parts of the causal argument.
representative_people.works: Queen Victoria: Gender and Power (1990)

verification.note: Complete Spanish translation 143–147 read from institutional PDF, including original-title and translator footnote. Journal page corroborates 1955 Hamish Hamilton original, 1–7; repository and journal disagree on issue numbering, so citation uses volume 4. Pages 143–144 explicitly discuss Graham Wallas and caution against unqualified psychological speculation; 145–147 discuss mass movements and political ideas. English original and historical examples not independently collated. This later translation is not the 1929 Structure of Politics, which remains unexamined in full.

added.title: Gordon S. Wood, “Rhetoric and Reality in the American Revolution,” William and Mary Quarterly 23.1 (1966), 3–32; reprinted in American Themes: Essays in Historiography (1968), 55–80.
added.citation: Gordon S. Wood, “Rhetoric and Reality in the American Revolution,” William and Mary Quarterly 23.1 (1966), 3–32; reprinted in American Themes: Essays in Historiography (1968), 55–80.

verification.note: Read primary opening 55, selected 69–78 and abridged notes 79–80 in 1968 reprint OCR at https://dokumen.pub/american-themes-essays-in-historiography.html . Title/imprint and reprint notice checked; original journal issue metadata corroborates 1966, 3–32. Wood 71–73 explicitly contrasts Namier with Bailyn and qualifies the criticism by setting; 75–78 proposes Virginia social strains. Reprint annotation is abridged and its note 16 includes the later 1967 Bailyn book; no claim of identical 1966 wording throughout. Original PDF downloads failed; no visual collation or original pamphlet/record audit.

outcomes.finding: Namier’s complete 1955 essay in a 2000 Spanish translation gives his own qualified treatment of conscious and unconscious motives, mass movements and psychological evidence. Wood’s 1966 intervention, read in a 1968 reprint, explicitly questions transferring Namier’s treatment of ideas to revolutionary America while retaining the value of his English setting. Wood’s reading of Bailyn connects political ideas to social situations and unintended outcomes; collective biography remains a useful technique without certifying universal claims about motives.
outcomes.research_limit: Namier read in Horacio Pons’s complete translation, not collated with English original or the full 1929 book. Wood: opening and selected 69–78 plus abridged notes 79–80 of 1968 reprint; original 1966 article not visually collated. This is a contemporary intervention in the wider methodological debate, after Namier’s death, not a personal reply during his lifetime. Butterfield 1957 article download returned 403 normally and on authorized retry; his book body remains unread. Colbourn’s complete 1959 review of Butterfield was consulted as background, not substituted for Butterfield’s own text. No complete account of popular participation or original parliamentary/pamphlet audit.
